clue.text: Picked one — a troublemaker!

parts.note: to pick one, in the idiom, is to start a quarrel deliberately, which is what a troublemaker does

explanation.surface: Someone chosen from a line-up turns out to be a nuisance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picked one' reads as 'chosen one', but the idiom is 'picked a fight', so 'one' stands for the brawl itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A brawl is what you have picked when you deliberately provoke a quarrel, as troublemakers do.

clue.text: They hold back their supplies of liquid until opening-time!

definitions.text: They hold back their supplies of liquid until opening-time!

parts.words: They hold back their supplies of liquid until opening-time!
parts.note: suggests landlords refusing drinks before the pub opens, but these barriers hold back water until they are opened

explanation.surface: Publicans refuse to serve drinks before the bar opens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening-time' is when British pubs open; here it is just the moment the sluices are raised.
explanation.definitionFit: Sluices on a river or canal hold back water until they are raised to release it.

clue.text: It's for holding up an order from the Queen

definitions.meaning: a band worn round the leg to keep a stocking from falling
the Most Noble Order of the ..., the senior English order of chivalry, bestowed by the monarch

explanation.surface: Something that stalls a royal command.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holding up' and 'order' look like delay and command; one is a stocking band, the other a knighthood.
explanation.definitionFit: A leg band holds up stockings, and the same word names England's senior order of knighthood.

clue.text: They're expected to be true to form!

definitions.text: They're expected to be true to form!

parts.words: They're expected to be true to form!
parts.note: true to form means behaving as usual, but a form is also a school class

explanation.surface: People who are predictable in their behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Form' is a British school class; staff are expected to be loyal to their class.
explanation.definitionFit: School staff are each in charge of a class, known in Britain as a form.

clue.text: May be dictated to by even the most easy going employer

definitions.text: May be dictated to by even the most easy going employer

parts.words: May be dictated to by even the most easy going employer
parts.note: dictated to suggests being bossed about, but an office assistant literally takes dictation of letters

explanation.surface: Even a relaxed boss sometimes lays down the law to staff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dictated to' sounds like tyranny, which jars with 'easy going'; the literal sense is having letters read out for taking down.
explanation.definitionFit: An office assistant traditionally took down letters spoken by the boss, so is dictated to in the literal sense.

clue.text: Used to sell theatre seats

definitions.meaning: market booths are used by traders to sell goods
the seats on the ground floor of a British theatre

explanation.surface: Theatre tickets that were sold secondhand.
explanation.walkthrough: In British theatres the seats on the main floor nearest the stage are named this way.
explanation.definitionFit: Market booths are used for selling, and the same word names the ground-floor seating in a theatre.

clue.text: Gathers they are parts of church services

definitions.meaning: brings together, as in assembling things

definitions.text: they are parts of church services
definitions.meaning: short prayers said in the liturgy, especially in the Anglican service

explanation.surface: A congregation assembles because church services require it.
explanation.walkthrough: As nouns, stressed on the first syllable, these are the short set prayers of the day in the Anglican prayer book.
explanation.definitionFit: To gather is to assemble, and the noun names short liturgical prayers in church services.

clue.text: Last to stand!

definitions.meaning: last as a verb means continue or survive
to stand something is to tolerate it

explanation.surface: The final one standing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last' looks like 'final'; it is the verb, to keep going.
explanation.definitionFit: To last is to survive over time, and to stand a hardship is to bear it.

clue.text: Don't want to get on without it

definitions.text: Don't want to get on without it

parts.words: Don't want to get on without it
parts.note: suggests not coping without something, but get on means advance in life, which needs drive

explanation.surface: Someone says they cannot manage without a thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get on' reads as 'manage'; it means succeed, and the desire to succeed is what is missing.
explanation.definitionFit: Drive or aspiration is the wish to get on in the world; without it you do not want to.

clue.text: The thread of a story?

parts.note: the thread of a story is its plot line, but literally the word is both spun fibre and a tall tale

explanation.surface: Someone asks what the plot line of a narrative is.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that one word means both spun thread and a long rambling story.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means spun fibre used for knitting and also an anecdote or tall tale.

clue.text: Deludes us, by the look of it

definitions.text: Deludes us, by the look of it

parts.words: Deludes us, by the look of it
parts.note: by the look of it usually means apparently, but here it means through what the eye sees

explanation.surface: Someone seems to be fooling us.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By the look of it' reads as 'apparently'; read literally it says the deception works through sight.
explanation.definitionFit: A trick of the eye misleads the viewer through vision itself, which is exactly deceiving by appearance.

clue.text: Beds down in the open here

definitions.text: Beds down in the open here

parts.words: Beds down in the open here
parts.note: beds down suggests someone sleeping rough, but flower beds are laid out in the open air

explanation.surface: A camper settles for the night under the stars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beds down' looks like a verb for sleeping outdoors; it is plural flower beds, set down outside.
explanation.definitionFit: Cultivated plots around a house contain flower beds laid out in the open air.

clue.text: Shopped for dealing. in drugs, amongst other things!

definitions.text: Shopped for dealing. in drugs, amongst other things!

parts.words: Shopped for dealing. in drugs, amongst other things!
parts.note: shopped for dealing suggests being informed on to police, but the clue means a shop that deals in medicines

explanation.surface: Someone was grassed up to the police for selling narcotics, among other crimes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shopped' is British slang for betrayed to the police; here it simply means visited as a shop, a pharmacy selling medicines and toiletries.
explanation.definitionFit: A British pharmacist's shop sells medicines alongside toiletries and other goods, so customers shop there for drugs among other things.

clue.text: Glassy-eyed children are often fond of them

definitions.text: Glassy-eyed children are often fond of them

parts.words: Glassy-eyed children are often fond of them
parts.note: glassy-eyed seems to describe the children, but describes the soft toys with glass eyes

explanation.surface: Dazed youngsters have their favourite comforts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Glassy-eyed' appears to qualify 'children'; it belongs to the toys, which had glass button eyes.
explanation.definitionFit: Stuffed toy bears often have glass eyes and are much loved by young children.

clue.text: They write depressing letters

parts.note: depressing reads as gloomy, but the writers press down the keys bearing letters

explanation.surface: Some correspondents send nothing but miserable news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depressing' looks like an adjective for sad letters; it is the verb, pushing down lettered keys on a machine.
explanation.definitionFit: Keyboard operators produce text by pressing down keys, each marked with a letter.

clue.text: They dissolve in solution, as it were!

definitions.text: They dissolve in solution, as it were!

parts.words: They dissolve in solution, as it were!
parts.note: dissolve in solution sounds like chemistry, but difficulties vanish once a solution is found

explanation.surface: A chemistry note about substances dissolving in liquid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Solution' sounds chemical; 'as it were' admits it is an answer to a difficulty.
explanation.definitionFit: Difficulties disappear once an answer to them is found, which is a solution in the other sense.

clue.text: Is inclined to believe posse's up and about

indicators.note: about signals the letters are moved around into a new order

parts.note: posse's gives the letters of posses, the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A sheriff's gang is awake and moving around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up and about' looks like a phrase for out of bed; 'about' alone is the anagram signal on POSSESUP.
explanation.definitionFit: To be inclined to believe something is to assume or think it likely.

clue.text: Marked dates in the wrong order…

indicators.note: putting the letters of these words in the wrong order rearranges them

explanation.surface: Someone noticed the dates had been written out of sequence.
explanation.definitionFit: Something soiled or discoloured has been marked with spots.

clue.text: Unhealthy conditions caused by new-fangled meal-tins

indicators.note: new-fangled suggests the letters given a new form, a rearrangement

explanation.surface: Food in modern tins is blamed for causing sickness.
explanation.definitionFit: Illnesses and disorders are unhealthy conditions of the body.

clue.text: Rose being disappointed on a date!

definitions.meaning: rose means got to one's feet
a person whose date never turns up has been let down this way

explanation.surface: Rose, a woman whose date never arrived.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rose' poses as a woman's name; it is the past tense of rise.
explanation.definitionFit: To have got up is to have risen, and to be jilted by a no-show date is the same phrase.

clue.text: A way through winding Eastern field

indicators.note: winding suggests twisting the letters into a new order

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for East

explanation.surface: A path snakes through a field to the east.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Winding' rearranges E plus FIELD to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrow pass through mountains is a way through difficult terrain.

clue.text: It's the rest of the workforce

definitions.text: It's the rest of the workforce

parts.words: It's the rest of the workforce
parts.note: the rest suggests the remainder of the staff, but it means the break workers take

explanation.surface: A remark about the remaining employees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The rest of' reads as 'the remainder of'; it is the rest, or break, that workers enjoy.
explanation.definitionFit: Time off from work is the rest, in the sense of relaxation, that employees are given.

clue.text: What reduces some intense dislike

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A question about what lessens strong animosity.
explanation.definitionFit: Loathing is a strong, intense dislike of someone or something.

clue.text: Spent force in America

parts.note: a spent force is something exhausted, but here it is money that is spent in the United States

explanation.surface: Something in the United States has lost all its power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spent force' is an idiom for something past its best; read literally it is currency that gets spent and is powerful in America.
explanation.definitionFit: The US currency unit is spent by Americans and wields economic force.

clue.text: To escape from police custody, it seems, is totally unexpected

definitions.text: To escape from police custody, it seems
definitions.meaning: to bolt is to run off, and the blue is the police, so this reads as fleeing the force
describes something arriving without warning, like a sudden thunderbolt

explanation.surface: A breakout from a police cell takes everyone by surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: The police are 'the boys in blue', so literally the phrase describes running away from them.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a sudden surprise, like lightning from a clear sky.

clue.text: Attempt to get round the Pole ends in tie!

indicators.note: the attempt is made to go around the pole, enclosing it

parts.note: a bid is an attempt
N stands for the North Pole

explanation.surface: An expedition trying to reach the Pole ends in a stalemate.
explanation.definitionFit: To bind is to tie something tightly together.

clue.text: Set people apart from the crowd!

definitions.text: Set people apart from the crowd!

parts.words: Set people apart from the crowd!
parts.note: set apart from the crowd suggests distinguishing someone, but literally means the crowd was broken up

explanation.surface: An instruction to make certain people stand out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set apart from the crowd' sounds like singling someone out; the literal sense is people scattered by breaking up a crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: A crowd that has been scattered has had its people separated from each other.

clue.text: Emergency call about the engineer — his boils, perhaps

indicators.note: the distress call is placed around, or about, the engineer

parts.note: SOS is the international distress signal
RE stands for the Royal Engineers, a British Army corps

explanation.surface: A sailor sends a distress call about the ship's engineer and his painful boils.
explanation.definitionFit: Boils are one example of inflamed painful spots on the skin.
